# ADDITIONS,
## & Notice to the Reader.

It is not due to an itch for writing, Dear Reader, that I present these *Curiosities* <note>Referring to the title of his work, *Curiositez inouyes*</note> to you; those who know me find that I am free from this foolish passion. A person of rank, to whom it is a crime to refuse anything he desires, has drawn them from my study, from which they would never have emerged; for after suffering so many slanders, I had intended never to publish anything in public again, having a thousand times sighed those words, once common to a Roman Prince: *If only I had never known letters!* <note>original: "utinam nescissem litteras!" A phrase attributed to the Emperor Nero, expressing a wish that he were illiterate so he would not have to sign death warrants; here, Gaffarel uses it to express his weariness with the world of scholarship and criticism.</note> But at last, prayers and commands have overcome my resolution. I have been coerced, I admit it, because I foresaw well that my enemies would not be able to stomach this other trial of my pen: but after all, I have cause for joy, since one of the great Prelates of our Century <term>Prelate: a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop</term> has condemned their insolence. Receive this work then with favor, dear Reader, and remember what we are: I mean to say that you will not find it perfect, because I am not an Angel; and if there is some flaw, one must blame our mortality, which causes all the rest of men to err.

<summary>Gaffarel explains to the reader that he published this work only at the insistence of a powerful patron, having previously resolved to stop writing due to public slander. He humbles himself by acknowledging his human imperfections while noting that his work has the backing of a high-ranking Church official.</summary>
<keywords>Jacques Gaffarel, preface, patronage, authorship, slander, Roman Prince, mortality, 17th-century publishing</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Gaffarel’s address to the reader. Following his explanation that he was pressured into publishing by a patron, he now defends his character as a scholar and justifies why a member of the clergy is writing about "bold" subjects like magic and astrology by citing prestigious historical precedents.</meta>

->Additions<-

Above all, know that I am not stubborn, nor have I ever been: I take the warnings given to me in very good part, and I do not consider myself so learned that I do not offer myself to be taught. It is only the foolish and the prideful who refuse it, and only the ignorant who claim to know everything. For my part, dear Reader, provided that you treat me as a friend, I ask for nothing else.

Now, if you find it strange that a clergyman like myself treats a subject so daring and so free-thinking, it seems, I pray you consider that many of my profession have put forward things much more liberal than these, and which are even judged dangerous. Thus, the Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a Benedictine abbot whose works on "steganography" or secret writing were often accused of being a cover for summoning spirits.</note> published his *Polygraphia* and his *Steganographia*, where the calling forth of spirits is manifest, although he uses them in a manner other than that of a sorcerer. William, Bishop of Paris, did not only write about **Natural Magic**, but knew and practiced it perfectly, according to the report of the great Pico, Count of Mirandola. <term>Natural Magic: A medieval and Renaissance branch of science that sought to use the inherent, hidden powers of nature—such as herbs, stones, or stars—without resorting to demons.</term> And another learned Bishop, Albert the Great, taught its foundations with great admiration. Roger Bacon and Jean de Roquetaillade, both Franciscan friars, did the same. Pedro Ciruelo, a Spaniard of the same order, showed to Christendom a large-format book on the four principal types of **Divination**, and all the maxims of **Judicial Astrology** <term>Judicial Astrology: The practice of using the positions of the stars to predict specific human events or personal destinies, which was often viewed with suspicion by the Church.</term>; Cardinal d'Ailly, Bishop of Cambrai, treated the same subject, as did Francesco Giuntini, a Priest.

<summary>Gaffarel defends his open-mindedness as a scholar and provides a list of high-ranking churchmen and theologians who previously studied magic and astrology to justify his own work. He argues that his interest in these "bold" subjects follows a long tradition of intellectual inquiry within the Church.</summary>

...Florentine, and Doctor of Theology: and since we are discussing the Italians, have not Aurelius Augurellus and Pantheus—both Priests, one a Venetian and the other from Treviso—described the fantasies of the **Philosopher's Stone**, the former in his *Gold-making* <note>original: *Chrysopoeia*, a poem by Augurellus (c. 1441–1524) dedicated to Pope Leo X about the art of making gold.</note> and the latter in his *Voarchadumia* <note>Giovanni Agostino Panteo's 1530 work on alchemy and metallurgy.</note>? What superstitions did Marsilio Ficino—also a Priest—not put forward? Indeed, what superstition is there in the world that he has not brought to light? Antonio Bernardi of Mirandola, Bishop of Caserta, following his example in his book on *Single Combat* <note>original: *De singulari certamine*.</note>, defended an infinity of things entirely contrary to our Religion; Cardinal Cajetan of Vio did the same; and Giovanni Ingegneri, Bishop of Capo d'Istria, recently amused himself by defending the foundations of **Physiognomy** <term>Physiognomy: The pseudo-scientific practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance, especially the face.</term>; and before all of these, Synesius, a Christian Bishop, wrote a book on the *Interpretation of Dreams*, later commented upon by another Bishop or Patriarch of Constantinople, Nicephorus Gregoras. I shall pass over the superstitions of the Abbot Joachim <note>Joachim of Fiore (c. 1135–1202), known for his apocalyptic prophecies.</note> and of Savonarola, a Dominican Monk; the *Asolani* <note>A series of dialogues on love by Cardinal Pietro Bembo.</note> of Cardinal Bembo; the *Lucretia* <note>A reference to the erotic epistolary novel *The Tale of Two Lovers*.</note> of Aeneas Silvius, who later became Pope Pius II; the book filled with vulgarities by Poggio the Florentine, Apostolic Secretary; I shall also pass over the *Macaronic History* <note>A satirical style of writing that mixes Latin with vernacular languages.</note> under the name of Merlin Coccai, written by Teofilo Folengo, a Benedictine Monk, and an infinity of other books written by Churchmen. If you happen to compare my own work with these, dear Reader, you will find—

...you will see that he is wrongly blamed. And so that you may be informed of my design, know that I do not grant any more faith to all these Curiosities than what the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman Church allows, and that I have only put forward at least some of the more sensitive ones after several Christians of my profession <note>Gaffarel was a priest and scholar; he is emphasizing that he follows a tradition of learned clergy.</note>, as you will be able to see. Regarding the calves of Jeroboam <note>Jeroboam was the first king of the northern Kingdom of Israel; he famously set up two golden calves at Dan and Bethel.</note>, I am not the first who has said that their construction was legitimate, and that this King was not an idolater: our learned Genebrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a famous French Benedictine exegete and Hebraist.</note> cleared the path for me, and after him Monceau <note>François de Monceau, who wrote a 1587 treatise arguing the golden calves were intended as symbols of God's presence, similar to the Cherubim, rather than false idols.</note> and before them Abiudan, and I am ready to withdraw from their company if it proves dangerous to me in this matter. Now, if you say that these Curiosities should not then have been called **UNHEARD-OF**, since others have treated them, I will answer you that the greatest part were **UNHEARD-OF** to Christians, since I draw them from the Hebrews, among whom they were so obscure that even those of that nation neglected them. As for Talismanic figures, they were so unheard-of in our century that even the name was not known: Now, so that you may have a more perfect knowledge of them, please add what follows.

In the first part, chapter 1, I say that I had not been able to find the reason why Plutarch, Strabo, Trogue, Tacitus, and Diodorus <note>A list of major Greco-Roman historians: Plutarch, Strabo, Trogus Pompeius, Tacitus, and Diodorus Siculus.</note> had accused the Jews of having worshiped a Vine-stock; I have since found that it was because they had...

...heard tell, and even seen—at least some of them—that in the Temple of Jerusalem there was a Golden Vine, with its branches and shoots set against the wall, just as Josephus describes it: "The inner gate," he says, "was entirely gilded, as I have said, and around it was a gilded wall; above it, moreover, it had golden vine-shoots, from which clusters of grapes the height of a man hung down." <note>original: "Interior porta, dit-il, tota inaurata, vt dixi, & circū eam auratus paries, deſuper autē habebat aureos Pampinos, vnde racemi ſtatura hominis dependebant." Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian whose descriptions of the Temple are the most detailed surviving accounts.</note> I know well that many have interpreted Josephus's words to mean that this Vine was not of massive and solid gold, but only painted, or decorated in the Phrygian style <note>The "Phrygian style" refers to "opus Phrygium," a type of ornate embroidery or superficial gold-work; Gaffarel is arguing against the idea that the vine was merely a decoration rather than solid metal.</note>. But the other Joseph, son of Gorion, objects to this interpretation: for speaking in the same history—and more clearly, and at greater length—about this golden Vine and its clusters, he says: <margin>Book 5, ch. 24.</margin> "Herod made, in addition, a vine of pure gold, and placed it upon the top of the columns, the weight of which was a thousand talents of gold. The vine itself was made with ingenious workmanship, having intertwined branches; its leaves and buds were made of shining gold, the clusters of tawny gold, and its grains, berries, and husks were made of precious stones; and the whole work was fashioned with varied skill, so that it was a marvelous sight and a joy of heart to all who saw it." <note>original: "fecit inſuper Herodes vitē de auro mundo, & poſuit in ſummitatem columnarum cuius pondus erat mille talentorum aureorum... etc." Joseph ben Gorion, or Josippon, is a 10th-century chronicler whose work was often mistaken in the Renaissance for a primary account by a contemporary of Josephus.</note> And then he adds immediately: "Many Roman writers also testify that they saw it when the Temple was being destroyed." <note>original: "Multi quoque ſcriptores Romani teſtantur ſe eam vidiſſe cum deſolaretur Templum."</note> Now the aforementioned authors—Plutarch, Plato, and the others—seeing that in the Temple there was a golden Vine so rich, so precious, and so admirable, they believed that the Jews worshipped it in honor of Bacchus <note>Bacchus (Dionysus) was the Greco-Roman god of wine and theater; ancient historians often tried to explain foreign religions by linking them to their own gods.</note>, who first had subjugated the East; this is the opinion of Cornelius Tacitus, who lived at the time...

In Constantinople, one also sees on a slab of sawn white marble the image of Saint John the Baptist, clothed in a camel skin, though with the natural defect that nature gave him only one foot. In Ravenna, in the Church of Saint Vitale, one can still see a Franciscan monk <note>original: "Cordelier." These were Franciscan friars, so named in France because of the knotted cord they wore as a belt.</note> naturally depicted on an ash-colored stone. In Schneeberg, Germany, there was found in the earth a small statue of a certain unrefined metal, naturally formed, which represented in the round a man having a small child on his back; and whoever has seen a painting of Saint Christopher can easily conceive of this one. Not long ago, in the Hercynian forest <note>The Hercynian forest was a vast, ancient forest region in central Germany often associated with mystery and folklore.</note>, a stone was found that naturally bore the figure of an old man with a long beard, crowned with a triple Tiara <note>The "triple Tiara" refers to the *triregnum*, the crown worn by Popes.</note>, exactly like the Roman Pontiff. Note also that several of these stones or <term>Gamahez</term> <note>Gamahez (or gamahés) are stones that naturally feature images or signatures, which Gaffarel believed held astrological or occult significance.</note> always share the same name because they always possess the same shape. Thus, the stone representing human eyes is called <term>Leuchoptalmos</term> <note>From the Greek *leukos* (white) and *ophthalmos* (eye).</note>; the one bearing a heart, <term>Encardia</term> <note>From the Greek *en* (in) and *kardia* (heart).</note>; the one shaped like a tongue, <term>Glossopetra</term> <note>From the Greek *glossa* (tongue) and *petra* (stone). These were often fossilized shark teeth, though Gaffarel views them as natural mineral formations.</note>; the one on which the male organs are depicted, <term>Enorchis</term> <note>From the Greek *en* (in) and *orchis* (testicle).</note>; and the one representing both the private parts of a man and a woman, <term>Diphys</term> <note>From the Greek *diphues*, meaning "of double nature" or "hermaphroditic."</note>, and so on. To the figures of planets and flowers, one can likewise add those that bear some species of letters and words, such as the Hyacinth stone, upon which the Poet says one can see written the lament of the beautiful Phoebus <note>Phoebus is another name for the Greek god Apollo.</note> for having...

The Author removes the suspicion that one might have regarding everything he teaches. The Researches that we will treat hereafter are so new that I have no doubt in calling them unheard-of <note>The title of the book, *Curiositez Inouyes*, uses this word to signal groundbreaking or rediscovered knowledge</note>. It is necessary then, to protect them from suspicion, that I take the side of the <term>Orientals</term> <note>A term used in the 17th century to refer to peoples of the Near East, particularly the Hebrews, Persians, and Arabs</note>, and principally the <term>Hebrews</term> who are their Authors, and that in matters of curiosities, I defend their innocence, which has been oppressed until now.

<margin>The response to the last three objections is in the following chapter.</margin>

1. One ordinarily abhors this nation for four reasons: The first, because of the idolatry of which authors make them guilty; the second, for the daydreams <note>original: "resveries"; meaning fantastical or nonsensical stories often attributed to the Talmud or Kabbalah</note> with which their books are filled; the third, because of the blasphemies they still vomit against Jesus Christ; and the last, for the errors they advance against the Law. The first is founded on a false belief: for since people imagined that the Jews worshiped the head of an Ass, Pigs, and Clouds, their books consequently cannot be exempt from these impieties. The second is based on the little knowledge one has of their writings; the third, on the hatred borne toward their Authors; and the fourth, on the stubbornness of those who accuse them.

<margin>Response to the first objection.</margin>
But let us here teach these ancient writers, since they have so often taught us: and would to God it had always been truths they taught. If it is true that the Jews abandoned themselves to the insolence of the idols we have just named, why did their legitimate God not rebuke them for it in the Scriptures He gave them, as He did for other crimes? And here one cannot say what we say of our own books—that a thing may have occurred even if they make no mention of it—but in this Law, which everyone recognizes as being very severe, it is not the same; for in matters of crimes, it has not concealed even the smallest. One cannot say either that this idolatry happened after the history of the Old Testament: For besides the fact that the enemies of the Jews would have reproached them for it as something most abominable, the aforementioned Authors claim that the law against eating pork was only given to them because they had worshipped that animal; but why have they not likewise asserted that this people had worshipped Rabbits, Hares, Camels, Ostriches, and Ravens, since they were also forbidden from eating them?

As for the **Golden Vine**, and the honors they are said to have rendered to **Bacchus** <note>The Roman god of wine; ancient historians often confused the decorative golden vine in the Temple of Jerusalem with Bacchic symbols</note>, I can find the source for this in no author. One can more easily notice the cause of the error regarding the **Clouds**, and that cloud which, being luminous on one side and dark on the other, miraculously guided the children of Israel through the deserts. Another reason I have just thought of will perhaps satisfy more: that the Jews were called <term>Heaven-worshippers</term> <note>original: "Coelicolae"</note>, as adorers of the Clouds or the Sky, because they worshipped God, who is often called in the Hebrew language **Heavens** <note>original: "שמים schamaim"</note>, a word which also signifies the Sky. As for the **head of an Ass**, those who trace the origin to the idea that Asses performed great services for the Hebrew people when they left **Egypt**, seem to be dreaming rather than speaking with any appearance of truth. And **Tacitus** <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56 – c. 120 AD), a Roman historian who famously recorded several anti-Jewish legends in his *Histories*</note> seems to me most ridiculous when he says that the Jews worshipped Asses, because they...

I much prefer to say, then, that the love of one's own religion has always been so passionate in everyone that those of different beliefs often resorted to insults for the slightest reason. Thus, if the Jews—either for being burdened with many laws or for being obedient to their God—were called "Asses" (just as the Emperor **Charles V** used to call the French "asses" because they are so remarkably compliant to their Kings), the early Christians were not exempt from this insult either. Indeed, their common nickname was <term>Ass-worshippers</term> <note>original: "Asinarij"</note>, according to the account of **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD)</note>. It went so far that a certain Prince, whose excessive hatred for Jesus Christ made him known as the most insolent man who ever lived, set up a statue in the form of an ass. He had it hold a book with the nail of its hoof, bearing the inscription: *The God of the Christians, the Donkey-Hoofed.* <note>original: "Deus Christianorum Ononychitis." This refers to the "Alexamenos graffito" or similar Roman-era caricatures mocking Christian worship.</note>

This Calf or Cherub was thus made; not that Aaron first melted the gold into a mass and then shaped it as sculptors do a mass of stone, as the aforementioned Moncæus suggests; nor did this Calf come about by chance, without Aaron having the intention to make a Calf, as many of the Ancients have asserted; but rather, having previously formed a mold: "And I cast it [the gold] into the furnace, and there came out this calf." <note>original: *Et proieci illud (aurum) in fornacem, egressusque est hic vitulus.* From Exodus 32:24.</note> If the people later angered God, it was not for having made this Calf, but for having worshiped it: for as Martial says:

> *He who fashions sacred faces in gold or marble*
> *Does not make them gods: he who prays to them, makes them.*

And we do not read that God ever rebuked Aaron for having made it.

Why then are the Rabbis blamed, who are clear of these follies?

3. Let us add further: almost all the Church Fathers held that one could read the books of the Pagan Philosophers; Saint Augustine and Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–c. 458 AD) was an influential theologian of the School of Antioch.</note> provide reasons for this that even the most critical are forced to admit. Now everyone knows that most of these books teach the plurality of Gods, and some even idolatry. But as for the books of the Hebrews, who is he who has ever accused them of these crimes, or who has noticed in them any doctrine other than that of the true God? Why then should the Learned not be able to read them, since we dare to expose others to the simplicity of children who are capable of believing anything? For even if one finds "fancies" in them—as those who have not read them object—they are not as dangerous as Apostasy, nor so absurd that one cannot draw something good from them, nor so barren that they are not accompanied by some good doctrine. Let us take the truths and leave the dreams, gather the roses and leave the thorns, collect the pearls and reject the shells; in a word, let us do what the blessed Damascene <note>Saint John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD), a Syrian monk and priest known for his defense of icons and his systematic theological works.</note> teaches: <note>original: *Si autem ab his qui foris sunt decerpere quippam vtile valuerimus, non aspernabile efficiamur probati Trapezitæ ligitimum & purum aurum aceruantis, adulterinum autem refutantes: sumamus sermones optimos, Deos autem ridiculos & fabulas alienas canibus proijciamus.*</note> "If, however," (he says) "we are able to pluck anything useful from those who are on the outside <note>Referring to non-Christians or those outside the Church.</note>, let us not be contemptible, but let us be like proven money-changers <term>Trapezitæ</term> <note>A term for money-changers or bankers who tested the purity of coins to distinguish genuine gold from counterfeit currency.</note> amassing legitimate and pure gold while rejecting the counterfeit: let us take the best discourses, but cast the ridiculous Gods and foreign fables to the dogs."

<margin>Fourth Objection.</margin>
9. I now touch upon the final Objection, which is that the books of the Rabbis err in the interpretation of the Law, and that being filled with vain, ridiculous, and even harmful Traditions, they should not be read by Christians, who ought to seek only the true Traditions of Jesus Christ and of his Church.

<margin>Response.</margin>
I do not wish to respond absolutely and in every respect to this objection, since it is certain that the Rabbis sometimes err and that they have very long-winded interpretations: but that for this reason they must be burned, or not read at all, is something that reason cannot suffer. Otherwise, we would be putting ourselves on trial and condemning our own books, which are almost none without error; I speak even of those which ought to be most necessary and commendable to us. Thus, if it were necessary to put them to the fire, we would soon see our libraries deserted, and those who would come after us...

And although <term>was</term> <note>original Greek: ἦν</note> signifies *it was* <note>original Latin: "erat"</note>: this way of speaking is nevertheless very elegant to use the imperfect tense for the present; and we can say in English *that which is the Being of the thing*.

7. In our time, another misunderstood text has given birth to yet another error, and not a minor one. It is based on the word <term>euoriston</term> <note>original Greek: εὐόριστον; meaning "easily bounded" or "easily defined."</note>: for when Aristotle, in the fourth chapter of the fourth book of the *Meteorology*, says: *The moist is most easily bounded by the boundary of another* <note>original Latin: "Humidum facillimè alieno termino terminari"</note>, or rather that it is <term>easily bounded</term>; it has been concluded from this that fire was moist, since it was easily bounded by another thing. The curious theses published a few years ago by a soldier from our Provence—who was otherwise a very fine philosopher—have made this proposition quite famous. But let us say what the truth teaches us: that when Aristotle says <term>easily bounded</term>, which is interpreted as *very easily* <note>original Latin: "prefacilé"</note>, he means *naturally* <note>original Latin: "naturaliter"</note>. Now, that fire cannot be naturally bounded is very certain from the experience of cannons and other fire-instruments <note>Refers to early modern artillery and firearms.</note>; for if this element is thus enclosed or bounded, it breaks [the container] or is itself broken. It is so true that a single misunderstood word often leads to very extravagant consequences.

<margin>Ethics, Chapter 4, and the Introduction on Difference.</margin>

<header>CURIOSITIES</header>

Philosophy cannot tolerate [the contrary opinion]. It must therefore be necessarily admitted, without me wasting time in proving it, that shape is a quality and not a quantity; and with this presupposed, let us debate whether shape acts and is capable of anything.

The conclusion we propose, and upon which everything we say in the next two Chapters will revolve, is this: *That shapes by themselves can do nothing, but when applied they can do something; or rather, they are "modificative,"* as the Scholastics <note>The "Schoolmen" or Scholastics were medieval theologians and philosophers who used Aristotelian logic to explain Christian doctrine.</note> say. This is the sentiment of Aristotle, which people have not yet been able to fully understand regarding shapes. Let us see what he says about it, and how he speaks of it.

10. There is nothing that more strongly condemns those who have maintained that these shapes could do nothing than the actual Greek text, properly understood, where this Philosopher speaks of quality: for he calls it <term>poiotēs</term> <note>original Greek: ποιότηϛ</note>, which is to say, *a faculty or ease of doing* <note>original Latin: "facultatem seu facilitatem faciendi"</note>, coming from the verb <term>poiein</term> <note>original Greek: ποιεῖν</note>, which means *to do* or *to make*. And the same Aristotle says that <term>poiotēs</term> <note>quality</note> makes us <term>poios</term> <note>original Greek: ποιὸϛ</note>, which is to say, *ready to act*, or as the learned interpret it, *Active* and *Effective*; for which reason Poets are called <term>poiētai</term> <note>original Greek: ποιηταὶ</note>, *makers of fables* <note>original Latin: "factores fabularum"</note>.

Since there are, then, four genres of quality: *Habit & Disposition; Affective Quality & Passion; Natural Power & Impotence; Form & Shape*; and since it is very certain that these are suited to doing something, or rather, as they say, *lead to action* <note>original Latin: "ad agendum conducunt"</note>—just as Habit leads to singing, Disposition leads to jumping, and so on for the others—

For if **Theology** teaches us, and reason confirms to us, that there is a certain providence which leads all things to their end, and which does nothing without design: why then do we wish to attribute to fortuitous chance that which makes us admire the power of **God**, and give over to hazard the most marvelous of things? Since, of all the many leaves seen in a forest, not one falls without the will of Him who created them. But whether one wishes to admit fortuitous figures or not, we shall nonetheless demonstrate the power of a great many which can only be called natural. Let us examine both kinds in order.

4. Regarding figures naturally engraved on stones, they are either engraved on the surface, or "openworked"—that is to say, the engraving passes all the way through. Of this kind, one often finds them among the piles of pierced stones in the countryside, in which one notices the shape of a head by the holes representing the eyes, nostrils, and mouth; often one also encounters those that have the figure of a skull, whether of a man or a horse. Regarding others that are simply engraved: see examples of them on river pebbles, and those found on the seashore, in which one can observe shells so well-made that one would say they are the natural shells of some fish; and this kind should rather be placed among the <term>Gamahez</term> <note>Stones naturally bearing the likeness of animals or objects.</note> in high relief <note>French: *en boſſe ronde*</note>, than simply engraved. 5. The most learned naturalists have divided them in this way. The plant, they say, is either a **tree**, or a **cliff-shrub**, or a **shrub**, or an **herb** <note>original Latin: *Arbor* or *Cremnum*, or *Frutex*, or *Herba*</note>. The tree is the plant that has a thick trunk and a large stem; the cliff-shrub <note>original: *Cremnum*</note> is that which has a small one; the shrub <note>original: *Frutex*</note> is that which has several stems; and the herb is when, beginning to show itself on the earth, it produces two small leaves. I find, therefore, in both kinds an infinity of admirable figures, which the philosophers have called the ***signatures of things*** <note>original Latin: *Signaturæ rerum*—the belief that the physical appearance of a natural object (like a plant) indicates its medicinal properties or its place in the cosmic order.</note>. Now, a shaped part of the plant, and not the whole plant, is called a *signature*; or rather, a signature is something within the part. I am not speaking of internal signatures—that doctrine belongs to the chemists <note>In this context, alchemists or early pharmacists who studied the "essence" of substances.</note>—I only put forward here those that are found on plants, which were little considered in past centuries. # CVRIOSITEZ
<note>Curiosities</note>

...order of the parts of plants, the signatures or marvelous figures that nature produces there.

Firstly, the root of several plants represents several parts of our body; thus that of the **Hermodactyl** <note>original: *Hermodacte*; likely the Tuberous Iris (*Iris tuberosa*), known as "Hermes's Finger" due to its root shape</note> bears the shape of a hand.

The stem is also admirable: for whether in those of large trees or small plants, one finds figures that represent those of animals: in the latter, the *Greater Snakeweed* <note>original: *Serpentaria maior*</note> perfectly resembles the skin of a snake, as do also the *Dragonstalk* <note>original: *Dracunculus*</note> and the *Serpent’s Garlic* <note>original: *Ophioscorodon*</note>. In the former, one must consider either the wood or the bark.

In the bark, one sometimes sees in that of old trees several figures representing various things through the variety of splits and crevices. In young trees that have smooth bark, these are marked by small traces, as if painted: and I once observed on the bark of a young cherry tree small trees laden with fruit so naturally expressed that it seemed as if a paintbrush had passed over it.

The wood seems more admirable, seeing as in many of them one sees the same things as in **Agates** <note>original: *Achates*; semi-precious stones often containing moss-like or landscape-like inclusions</note>. Thus, during the time I was studying in Apt, a city very famous in Provence for the sacred Relics that tradition alone assures us are those of Saint Anne, mother of the Blessed Virgin, I saw a vine stump that so naturally <note>original: *naïfuement*; here meaning realistically or lifelike</note> represented a man’s head that one could even see the hair; all the rest, such as the forehead, ears, eyes, nose, mouth, and chin, were of quite fair proportion. It was brought by a vine-grower into the shop of Mr. Roulet, a Master Surgeon.

The branches of the plant are less remarkable, regarding figures, than all the rest (unless it be within the wood); however, one often notices there the arrangement of the fingers of the hand, and the thickness of hair: and it is for this reason, in my judgment, that when Poets discourse in their Metamorphoses <note>a reference to Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, the classical Roman poem describing the transformation of humans into plants, animals, and stones</note> on the transformation of men into trees, they say that their fingers and hair were changed into branches. In those of coral, several curiosities have been seen often enough, and it is not so rare that one cannot experience it for oneself.

The leaves seem to surpass all the rest, being divided into so many figures that there seems to be nothing in nature whose image they do not bear: for, if it is a question of all the parts of the body, they represent them; if one can see waters there, one finds them wavy; if animals—

Fruits, because of their form and figure, are equally admirable; and although they do not represent as many things as leaves and flowers, they nonetheless represent several very significant ones, as seen in certain gourds, pears, apples, and other fruits. The peas called *Arietini* <note>Latin: "ram-like" (chickpeas)</note> represent the head of a ram, and others the head of a dove, called for the same reason *Columbini* <note>Latin: "dove-like"</note>, with this quality matching their appearance: that they are both equally "hot" <term>hot: a reference to the Galenic system of medicine, which classified plants by their "temperament" (hot, cold, moist, or dry)</term>. Beans bear on one side the shape and figure of the private parts of a man, and on the other those of a woman; and I know not if for this reason alone *Pythagoras* gave that advice which no one has ever been able to fully understand: *Abstain from beans* <note>original: *A fabis abstineto*; a famous and enigmatic taboo in Pythagorean philosophy</note>.

> *Just like the Borametz that among the Scythians are born*
> *From a tiny seed, and upon plants they feed:*
> *Though by the body, eyes, mouth, and nose*
> *They look like sheep that were but recently born.*

-># CURIOSITIES<-

Now, in all parts of plants, the figures are either external only, internal only, or both external and internal together. The internal ones are like that fruit of Palestine which bears the form of ashes within <note>A reference to the "Apples of Sodom," described by ancient historians as beautiful fruits that crumbled into smoke and ash when picked</note>, and all the figures that are found when sawing through marble. The external ones are like those that are painted and colored on the surface of fruits and not within, such as the Rambour apples <note>A variety of large cooking apple popular in the 17th century</note> spotted with red, appearing like drops of blood on the skin only. The external and internal together are found in the Maple and in several kinds of stones. Internal figures are further revealed by either an indiscriminate or a specific cut. The indiscriminate is like that sort of apple seen in Granada <note>The Spanish city of Granada</note>, according to the report of <margin>In *Fornicarius*</margin> Nider <note>Johannes Nider, a 15th-century Dominican theologian whose work *Fornicarius* (The Anthill) discussed wonders and morals</note>, which, when cut in any way whatsoever, always displayed a Crucifix. The specific cut is like the root of the Fern, which, when cut in only one way, perfectly represents the Eagle <note>The "Eagle Fern" (*Pteridium aquilinum*) shows a vascular pattern in its cross-section that resembles a double-headed eagle</note>. I have often observed that an Orange cut in this way—not crosswise, but lengthwise—represents in its seeds and membranes an Orange tree laden with its oranges. It has also been observed that apple seeds represent the tree itself. Figures also consist of either color or the division of parts: in color, such as the flower of Eyebright <note>original: *Euphraise*; a plant traditionally used for eye ailments because its flower markings resemble a bloodshot eye</note>, which represents all the parts of the eye; in the division of parts, such as those we have already seen.

This concludes the classification of figures; it remains now to prove that they possess some power, and

-># UNHEARD-OF CURIOSITIES<-

...that it is not in vain that they are perfectly represented both in plants and in stones. Let us follow in order the same division that we have made of them, beginning with the first.

6. I say, then, that the natural figures found in stones have naturally the power to act if they are applied: I prove this by two reasons. The first, because they are called *effectors* <note>The author uses the term "effectrices" to suggest these shapes are not just decorative but are the active "cause" of the stone's power</note>. The second, because experience teaches it: for one sees every day that some of these figured stones act upon the same things they represent, such as that which is called *Heliotrope* <note>original: *Heliotropius*; today commonly known as Bloodstone, a green chalcedony with red inclusions of iron oxide</note>, spotted with drops of blood; if it is applied to a bleeding part, it stanches the blood. Others act upon the wound made by the beast whose image they bear: thus Pliny <margin>Book 36, ch. 7</margin> assures us that one finds a kind of marble called *Ophites* <note>From the Greek *ophis*, meaning snake; likely Serpentine marble</note>, because it represents the very serpents whose name it bears; if this is applied to the bite of these beasts, it heals it. ...dispersed in the vial, one noticed a sort of small dark cloud which, dividing into several parts, finally came to represent a rose so beautiful, so fresh, and so perfect, that one would have judged it to be palpable and fragrant as one growing from a rosebush. This learned man said that he had often tried to do the same, and having failed through diligent effort, chance finally allowed him to witness this marvel. For while he was passing time with **Mr. de Luynes**, known as **de Formentières**, a Councilor in Parliament, observing the curiosity of several experiments, he had extracted the salt from certain burnt nettles and placed the lye <note>A liquid solution made by leaching the salts from the ashes of plants.</note> out in the night air <note>original: *serein*; refers specifically to the cold, damp evening air of a clear night.</note> in winter. In the morning, he found it frozen, but with this miracle: the species of nettles—their shape and their figure—were so naturally and perfectly represented on the ice that the living plants were no better. This man, being utterly delighted, called the aforementioned Councilor to witness this secret, the excellence of which led him to conclude with these words:

> *A secret from which we understand that, though the body dies,*
> *Forms still make their dwelling within the ashes.*
<note>original: *Secret dont on comprend que, quoy que le corps meure, / Les formes font pourtant aux cendres leur demeure.*</note>

->### EXTRAORDINARY <note>The header "INOVYES" is an archaic spelling of *inouïes*, part of the book's title, *Curiositez inouyes* (*Unheard-of Curiosities*).</note><-

...as ridiculous as the dreams of the Quran <note>original: *l'Alcoran*</note>. Our discourse will be woven only from the natural power that Images crafted under certain constellations can have, banishing from here all operation of demons, and all superstitious virtue.

I prove then this power of Figures and Images by three ways: by the influence of the Stars; by the virtue of resemblance; and by experience. I begin with the latter:

3. First, it is certain, and one cannot deny it without giving the lie to the most truthful Historians, that one has seen both in our days, and in those of our fathers, these Talismans or Talismanic Figures (as we shall now call them) which have cured the bites of serpents, scorpions, rabid dogs, and several other misfortunes that happen only too often. The ancient Arabs—such as Almanzor, Mashallah <note>original: *Messahallah*; an 8th-century Persian Jewish astrologer and astronomer.</note>, Sahl ibn Bishr <note>original: *Zahel*; a 9th-century astrologer and mathematician.</note>, Albohazen <note>Abū l-Hasan 'Alī ibn Abī l-Rijāl, a 10th-11th century Arab astrologer.</note>, Ali ibn Ridwan <note>original: *Haly Rhodoam*; a prominent 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer.</note>, Al-Battani <note>original: *Albatecnius*; a famous 10th-century astronomer.</note>, Umar al-Tabari <note>original: *Homar*.</note>, Zachdir, Hahamed, and Serapion—provide very true examples of this, for which reason Haly asserts: *A useful image of a serpent can be made when the moon enters the celestial serpent, or looks upon it favorably. Similarly, an effective likeness of a scorpion [can be made] when the moon enters the sign of Scorpio, etc.* <note>original Latin: *Vtilem serpentis imaginem effici posse, quando luna serpentem cælestem subit, aut fœliciter aspicit. **12.** **Astrology** also demonstrates the power of resemblance, judging the qualities of a child by those of the stars: for **Mars**, emitting a brilliant and red light, makes him who is born under its influence reddish. **Saturn**, which is pale and languid, makes him wan and discolored. **Jupiter** and **Venus**, darting clear, sweet, and pleasant rays, make him beautiful and pleasing. If, then, resemblance holds such power in everything we have just seen, let us conclude that it is no less significant in that of talismanic figures <term>talismanic figures: Objects engraved with specific symbols or characters during specific astrological alignments, believed to channel the power of the heavens.</term>; this is all the more certain because experience shows it to us. It remains now to prove this natural power through the third way, which is the virtue of the Stars: this will be easy if we first show the method that the most learned follow in preparing these Images. I say "the most learned," because I know that many do not make as many observations—as we shall see—even though they sometimes see the desired effect happen, though it takes more time.

17. First, one proposes the effect they wish to achieve with these images, such as driving away harmful animals, calming the violence of the winds, turning away lightning and hail, healing certain diseases, and other things. Once this is proposed, one seeks the proper means to reach this end. For example, to cure dropsy <term>dropsy: Historically called "hydropsy," this is the medical condition known today as edema, characterized by an accumulation of fluid in the body.</term>, one must consider that the disease consists of moisture; one must therefore choose not a random material to engrave and carve under the Constellations, but one already hot and dry by nature. Secondly, one must choose as the ascending sign one that is similarly hot and dry, such as Aries <note>original: "le belier"</note>. In the third place, one must also choose the sign to which this disease is subject, such as Saturn; but also having need of a very moist Star, so that the sympathy <term>sympathy: A concept in natural magic where objects with similar qualities or "signatures" are thought to naturally attract or influence one another.</term> which is so powerful in all—

19. Aristotle, to powerfully prove the affirmative, forms an admirable argument worthy of such a Philosopher. The other reason is that these things, when put to work, are crafted under certain constellations which infuse <term>influence: the astrological concept of celestial power "flowing into" terrestrial objects</term> them with qualities they did not have. Experience shows us this with a biscuit <note>Specifically hardtack or bread; the author is likely referring to the baker’s craft.</note>, where one will keep for a long time, while another baked either before or after is subject to worms and corruption, even though they are kept in the same place, made from the same wheat, kneaded with the same water, and prepared with every imaginable condition being equal. The marvelous effects that have always been observed in Talismanic Figures have so troubled the minds of those who categorize as Magic everything they cannot understand, that—without making a distinction between natural and lawful power and that which our faith makes us flee—they have boldly published that everything arising from these figures was diabolical. Alteration in this context refers to a change in the internal quality of a substance rather than its physical position.</note> I am surprised that this curious **Jesuit**, who was otherwise both very learned and a very good **Philosopher**—as there is no lack of them in that **Congregation**—did not nevertheless take care that he was sinning here against the maxims of **Philosophy** advanced by himself: for when he concedes that the figure is a co-principle in local motion and in the operations that occur by this motion, but not in those that occur by alteration, he con-

### CURIOSITIES

...concludes against what he himself has posed, since, following the consensus of all the **Philosophers** <note>Specifically the Scholastic philosophers who followed Aristotle’s teachings on physics</note>, **heat** is produced by **motion**. Now, heat is an **alteration** <term>alteration: in Aristotelian physics, this refers to a change in quality (like becoming hot) rather than a change in place or size</term>; therefore, the **figure** [shape] by itself is a **co-principle** <term>co-principle: a secondary cause that works alongside a primary one to produce an effect</term> to the operations that occur through alteration. Furthermore, when he concedes to **Cajetan** that if broad **iron** floats on **water**, he says it is not by reason of the figure, but of the **quantity** <note>Here "quantity" refers to the mass or bulk of the object</note>; these are his words: *But granted it happens, it will be not by reason of the figure, but by reason of the quantity*; <note>original: "Sed esto fiat, erit non ratione figuræ, sed ratione quantitatis"</note> yes, but according to his own logic and in sound Philosophy, *quantity is not active*: <note>original: "quantitas non est activa"</note> see what the consequence must be.

Finally, when **Cajetan** concludes that it is therefore the figure that causes the broad iron to float on the water, **Delrio** responds that this figure is only there by accident. For, he says, if one makes this iron which is broad and thin into another figure—circular, square, or pentagonal—it will always be the same; that is to say, it will float on the water, and therefore it acts only by accident. But he is mistaken: for **Cajetan's** intention is not to oppose a flat figure (or in **Mathematical** terms, *in a plane* <note>original: "In plano"</note>) to another figure that is also flat, whether it be square or circular; but rather to compare a flat figure to one that is **solid**.

For the flat one, be it square, circular, octagonal, or whatever it may be, will do something that the same figure, if it were solid, would not do. This is very true, since iron that is thick and square will sink to the bottom of the water, which the same iron will not do if it is thin and square. Therefore, it is a most certain maxim that the figure acts and can achieve an effect.

11. The other objections raised against the power of these images are reported and refuted by **Galeotus** <note>Galeotto Marzio (1427–1497), an Italian physician and humanist who wrote "De doctrina promiscua"</note>; these are the most pressing: In these images engraved on **gold**, which are made to counter the **stone** <note>kidney stones</note> and pain in the kidneys, gold by its nature does not heal the kidneys, and the image even less so—for being without life, it cannot alter the gold and make it pass into another nature. In the image, moreover, there is neither **action** nor **passion** <term>action and passion: in Scholastic physics, "action" is the power of one thing to affect another, and "passion" is the capacity to be affected or changed</term>: furthermore, gold itself, whether shaped or not, is always of the same species, and consequently the ray of the **Star** always acts in the same way; if it acted on shaped gold rather than simple gold, it would seem that this action proceeded from the **choice** of the heavens <note>meaning the stars would have to "choose" their targets, rather than acting naturally and uniformly</note> rather than anything else. And in short, the power given to this figure can be neither natural nor artificial: not natural, because it does not come from within; even less artificial, because the craftsman has not communicated it to it; it must therefore come from elsewhere.

The learned solution of **Galeotus** is this: "For in this matter, a change of species <note>a change in the fundamental nature or "essence" of the material</note> is not required, nor is the property of gold changed, nor does any choice by the heavens intervene, nor is that power of healing given by the craftsman, nor does the image as an image accomplish anything, etc. but it offers a principle of action and passion, as **Blessed Thomas** and **Albert the Great** <note>Thomas Aquinas and Albertus Magnus, two of the most influential medieval theologians and philosophers</note> testify: not as a figure and image perceived mathematically, but as it effects another preparation in the figured thing which may receive the celestial action without difficulty in various ways." <note>original: "Non enim in hac re mutatio speciei requiritur, nec proprietas auri immutatur, nec ulla cælorum electio interuenit, nec ab artifice vis illa sanãdi datur, nec imago ut imago quicquã efficit, &c. sed principiũ actionis ac passionis offert, ut beatus Thomas Magnusq; Albertus testantur: non ut figura & imago matematicè animaduersa, sed ut efficit aliam in re figurata præparationem quæ celestem actionẽ sine difficultate variis modis accipiat."</note> And then explaining how various figures, which are under the heavens, make some more

...naturally more suited than others to receive such influence; he brings the example of mirrors, of which the round concave ones receive the Sun’s rays so well that they burn, while others do not; thus the diversity of mountains and valleys is the cause of greater heat or cold. One can add pieces of ice, which the Sun cannot easily melt and dissolve if they are smooth, but very easily when they are rough. This is what led many to say that painted figures were not as suited to the subject we are treating as engraved or carved ones; which is true for gold: although the figure does not make it of another species <term>species: in Scholastic philosophy, the "species" is the essential nature or "kind" of a thing that defines what it is (e.g., gold), as opposed to its "accidents" like shape or temperature</term>, it nevertheless makes it more suited to such an action, just as hot and cold water are of the same species, yet one cooks meat and the other does not. This is why the same Galeotus concludes in these terms: *Therefore, a certain tempering of treatment is required in things of one and the same species, so that the effect may be varied.* <note>original Latin: "Requiritur ergo in vnius & eiusdem speciei rebus certum culturae temperamentum, vt varietur effectus."</note>

The Sun, shining then, struck the opposite horn; so that the shadow, falling upon the roundness of the ball—the height of which did not exceed that of the horns of the crescent—marked the hours distinctly until about ten of our hours. At that point, the Sun, being higher, could no longer strike the side of the horn to mark the following hours with its shadow; therefore, the circle <note>Likely the ring or hoop mentioned on the previous page as surrounding the ball.</note> compensated for this defect, marking the time almost until two o'clock in the afternoon. Afterward, as the Sun descended, the other horn of the crescent began to mark the time until night. Thus, of the twelve hours of the day, the circle always marked four, which were from ten o'clock until two o'clock in the afternoon; and this space of time is still called "Midy" <note>Midday or Noon.</note> by all the Orientals <note>A historical term for people of the Near East or Levant.</note>, who naturally divide the day into three parts: Morning, Midday, and Evening, having allowed the use of mechanical clocks to fall away, as **Scaliger** <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a renowned scholar of the Renaissance who studied ancient systems of timekeeping.</note> has remarked.

As for the hours of the night, they were known on this instrument by means of the Moon, shining upon a peg with which one plugged one of the holes in the circle each day. The hours were engraved around these holes; thus the peg, which passed through to the outside, served as a needle or pointer, which the Greeks call a <term>gnomon</term> <note>original Greek: **γνώμον**; the part of a sundial that casts a shadow to indicate the time.</note>. If I had not found some obscurity in this description, I would have included the diagram and the method for setting up the clock here; but I prefer to remain silent on things I do not clearly understand rather than to speak of them blindly. Perhaps a greater period of leisure will allow me to understand its secrets and describe them more fully.

The author concludes by admitting the complexity of the device, choosing to withhold a diagram until he can more accurately grasp its design.</summary>

# CURIOSITIES

If we did not know that in matters of doctrine—especially when it is ancient and curious—it is very difficult to grasp all its secrets without them being mingled with some fantasies, one would find it strange that I here disavow what Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a towering figure in Renaissance scholarship, known for his work on chronology and history.</note> (rightly held as the most learned man of our century) has established as most true within the tradition of the peoples of the Orient. But those who have read the books titled *The Flight of Mary*, *The Deeds of Joseph*, *The History of Kings*, *The Lots of the Apostles* <note>original titles: *Fuga Mariæ, De gestis Ioseph, Historia Regum, Sortes Apostolorum*. These were apocryphal texts—writings not included in the official Bible—often filled with legendary and supernatural accounts.</note>, and many others, will be able to judge that since even the holiest matters could not pass through the succession of centuries without some grotesque tales being created about them, there is more reason that those things which are of little consequence to us could not maintain the purity they possessed at their birth. 

The Astrology of the Hebrews had not yet lost much of its luster so long as only those of that nation practiced it; but ever since the Northerners <note>original: *Septentrionaux*. This refers to the scholars of Northern Europe, whom Gaffarel suggests misinterpreted the Semitic traditions.</note> gained some knowledge of it, they began to say such extravagant things about it, and to increase the number of fables to such an extent, that I am not at all surprised if this science is now discredited. This is why I consider it necessary, before descending to what we hold as pure and true, to touch upon what is false and corrupt; this we shall do by reporting a portion of what has been written by the same Scaliger, Riccius, Khunrath, Vigenère, and Duret.

Duret <note>Claude Duret (c. 1570–1611), a French magistrate and scholar whose work on the "History of Languages" Gaffarel is about to dismantle.</note>, it being afterwards very easy for anyone to recognize the deception in all the other authors of lesser consideration. The first, second, and third wrongly attribute to the Hebrews an Astrology which they never knew. The fourth makes them recognize, within the secrets of this science, spirits that never had any existence except in his imagination, and makes them the authors of an infinity of foolishness invented on this subject by the Greeks and Latins; and the last one constructs a phantom out of this entire doctrine, and concludes from it things so grotesque that they can easily be ranked alongside the *Fables of Merlin* <note>A reference to the legendary wizard; in 17th-century intellectual circles, "Merlin's fables" was a common idiom for absurd or nonsensical medieval folklore.</note>.

### CURIOSITIES

This Table seems difficult at first, but it is not at all so, if one considers that the seven letters of each row, moving from right to left or from left to right, mark the **seven Planets**; and these letters are the first initials of these complete words:

שבתאי <term>*Shabbatai*</term> <note>original: "Schautai"</note>, **Saturn**, Saturday.
צדק <term>*Tzedek*</term> <note>original: "Tſedeq"</note>, **Jupiter**, Thursday.
מאדים <term>*Maadim*</term> <note>original: "Maadim"</note>, **Mars**, Tuesday.
חמה <term>*Chamah*</term> <note>original: "Chamah"</note>, **The Sun**, Sunday.
נוגה <term>*Nogah*</term> <note>original: "Nogah"</note>, **Venus**, Friday.
כוכב <term>*Kokhav*</term> <note>original: "Cocau"</note>, **Mercury**, Wednesday.
לבנה <term>*Levanah*</term> <note>original: "Leuanach"</note>, **The Moon**, Monday.

Now if I want to know, for example, which Planet rules at the first hour of Saturday night—which is the hour that comes after the day of Saturday—I have recourse to the Table, where having found the letter **ש** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Shin', the initial for Saturn</note> which marks **Saturn**, I say that it is this Planet which rules at this hour; and then descending along the column of the same letter, I find that **Jupiter**, marked by **צ** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Tzadik'</note>, rules at the second hour; **מ** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Mem'</note>, that is to say **Mars**, rules at the third; **ח** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Het'</note>, the **Sun**, at the fourth; **נ** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Nun'</note>, **Venus**, at the fifth; **כ** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Kaf'</note>, **Mercury**, at the sixth; **ל** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Lamed'</note>, the **Moon**, at the seventh. And once again, **ש** Saturn at the eighth; **Jupiter** at the ninth; **מ** Mars at the tenth; **ח** the Sun at the eleventh; and finally **נ** Venus at the twelfth. In descending further through the same column, I find that **כ** Mercury rules at the first hour of the... <note>The text continues on the next page, likely transitioning to the first hour of the following day.</note>

I would have willingly asked him if this word is so ancient; is it then Greek, Hebrew, or Arabic? He was careful not to say, since he would have contradicted what he had taught. Let us then draw the truth from the Grave, and show in two words from whence comes this name *Athlon*, so long unknown. We have said that the ancient Hebrews related all the observations they made on Nativities <note>Birth charts or the positions of the stars at the moment of birth.</note> to twelve places, whether using some instrument or a simple figure. Rabbi Nathan accepted the term in that sense, saying that they tied the birth chart <term>Geniture</term> around the child’s neck—which Abarbanel shows to be false—but they were instead called *Machatalot* from the verb חחל *Hatal* <note>original Hebrew: חתל (*hatal*), meaning to wrap, swaddle, or bind.</note>, which means "to bind," because they were taken and considered together, as if bound and not disunited or separate. For if one left out even one of them, one could not judge the child’s fortune with perfection. 

Now, from this *Hatal* or *Machatalot*, through linguistic corruption, the word *Athlon* was formed, which Manilius alone used since he described Astrology according to the ancients. And that is the source of this word so sought after by Scaliger, who asserted it was unknown to the Hebrews. And these Signs are different from Hieroglyphs because Hieroglyphs represent things obscurely—as, for example, a battle represented by a sword—whereas these, on the contrary, represent them clearly, such as a battle represented by another battle. All these letters, marks, and Hieroglyphs are not only represented in the **Clouds**, but sometimes in all the rest of the <term>Meteors</term><note>original: "Metheores." In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain, snow, and lightning, not just falling stars.</note>; such as **Comets**, lightning, rain, hail, snow, **Manna**, and hoarfrost, as we shall see; beginning with the **Clouds**.

2. Now, whether these <term>portents</term><note>original: "prodiges"</note> occur naturally, or instead by the sole power of a God who warns us of our crimes, we shall resolve hereafter; suffice it to say that we do not fail to see the effect following the sign, to the astonishment of all those who reduce everything to the principles of **Philosophy** <note>Here, "Philosophy" refers to "Natural Philosophy," what we would now call science or secular logic.</note>. The **Second Rule** is that when the **Comet** or the fiery **Meteor** is round, clear, bright, and in no way dark—resembling a **Sun**—it can signify the birth of some great **Prince**. The **Third [Rule]** is that if these same **Comets** are shaped like a **Pyramid**, one will see damages caused by fire, and by **Analogy**, the effects of some **tyranny**. This is the opinion of **Cornelius Gemma** <note>A 16th-century physician and astronomer known for his work on celestial phenomena and their divine meanings.</note> who explains it in these words: <margin>On the Divine Characters of Nature.</margin> *Perhaps those which end in a sharp Pyramid signify more the predominance of fire, and by analogy, tyranny in the state.* <note>original Latin: "Fortassis quæ in acutam Piramidem desinunt, ignis prædominia magis, & ex analogia in republica tyrannidem præsignificant."</note>

### CHAPTER XIII.

### That the Stars, according to the Hebrews, are arranged in the Heavens in the form of Letters, and that one can read there everything of the greatest importance that occurs in the universe.

->SUMMARY.<-

1. *Celestial configuration of the Greeks permitted by the Church, although perilous. New doctrine of the reading of the Stars not repugnant to the faith.*
2. *This reading proved by Holy Scripture; interpretation of various passages on this subject.*

Those who have diligently examined the curious doctrine of the Ancients have found that there was nothing more seemingly absurd than the painting or configuration of the Heavens: For what confusion (they say) to house in these places, which are destined only for blessed spirits, animals so frightening that one cannot recall them to memory without horror. Yet, if one had granted a place there to mortals, and if one made a Castor and Pollux <note>Twin brothers from Greek mythology who became the constellation Gemini.</note> reign there, it would be necessary to blame love, which does not allow us to wish for anything but great blessings for those we love. This consideration similarly satisfied those who complained that the Heavens were depicted only with the crimes of Jupiter <note>The king of the gods in Roman mythology, whose myths often involved illicit affairs.</note>, and that everywhere one saw only marks of his incests.

# UNHEARD-OF CURIOSITIES <note>The header "INOVYES" is an archaic spelling of *Inouïes* (Unheard-of), part of the title of Jacques Gaffarel’s 1629 work on the "Celestial Alphabet."</note>

furthermore, why in the same word in this same **Writing** are there large and small letters or **Stars**? The answer is that it is to draw attention to the letters of the word that are more significant; this method being very well-known in the art of **anagrammatizing**. For instance, if in the word **Emperor** <note>original: *Empereur*</note>, I wish to highlight the word **FATHER** <note>original: *PERE*</note>, I will write the word **Emperor** in this fashion: em**PERE**ur, where the letters of the word **FATHER** are larger than the others. The same applies to this word, **Kingdom** <note>original: *Royaume*</note>, in which if I wish to highlight **ROME**, I will write the entire word as follows: **RO**yau**ME**. One must not, therefore, be astonished if in the Heavens we often see two or three large **Stars** composing a word where small ones are also found; and it is to this that one must particularly pay attention above all, as we have just said, when they are vertical <note>Meaning at the zenith, directly overhead a specific geographic location.</note>. In this way, one can provide a reason for that which is unknown; as when **Astrologers** assert that when the head of **Algol**, or **Medusa** <note>The star Algol, representing the head of the Gorgon Medusa in the constellation Perseus, traditionally associated with misfortune and violence.</note> was vertical over **Greece**, the **Stars** predicted to her the misfortunes that befell her through the tyranny of the **Mohammedans** <note>A reference to the conquest of Greece by the Ottoman Empire.</note>, without, however, giving any reason for it. # EXTRAORDINARY <note>original: "I N O V Y E S." This is the second half of the book's title, *Curiositez Inouyes* (Unheard-of Curiosities).</note>

V 2

...people to interpret that [writing] which one sees in the Sky, which is most often obscure and difficult; it being very necessary to interpret it perfectly to know **GEMATRIA**, **NOTARICON**, and **TEMURAH**, which are the three parts of the **Kabbalah** <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>A Jewish mystical system of thought that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal, mysterious Infinite and the finite universe.</note>. Of these, the first—the word for which, **Gematria** <note>original Hebrew: גמטריא</note>, is a corruption of the Greek word for **geometry** <note>original Greek: γεωμετρία</note>, or perhaps the latter is from the former—considers the numbers contained within letters. By comparing them with other similar numbers, the explanation of what was obscure results. An example is when it is said in Genesis regarding the coming of the Messiah <margin>Genesis 49:10.</margin> "**Shiloh shall come**" <note>original Hebrew: יבא שילה (*Ioua Schilo*)</note>; these Hebrew letters yield the number 358, which is the same number as the letters of the **Messiah** <note>original Hebrew: משיח (*Maschich*)</note>. For this reason, when the Prophet says: "**Until Shiloh comes**" <note>original Latin: *Donec venerit schilo*</note>, it is as if he had said: "**Until the Messiah comes**" <note>original Latin: *Donec venerit Meßias*</note>.

The second part is when the letters of a word each represent entire words, as in that motto of the Romans, **S.P.Q.R.**—"**The Senate and the People of Rome**" <note>original Latin: *Senatus Populuſq; Romanus*</note>—and in this Hebrew name of man, **ADAM** <note>original Hebrew: אדם</note>. In this, the first letter signifies **dust** <note>original Hebrew: אפר (*epher*)</note>; the second, **blood** <note>original Hebrew: דם (*dam*)</note>; and the third, **bitterness** <note>original Hebrew: מרה (*marah*)</note>. It is as if man were nothing but bitterness and pain, blood of corruption and vice, and after everything, but dust and ashes.

The third and last part (whose name **Notaricon** is likewise taken from the Latin **Notary** <note>original Latin: *Notarius*</note>, or else this from the Hebrew **to transfer** <note>original Hebrew: נתר (*Natar*)</note>, a word that is very well-suited to the art of **Anagrammatizing**), is when one or two words join together...

Now, to frankly express my opinion regarding this celestial writing <note>The "Celestial Alphabet," a theory that stars are arranged to form Hebrew letters that can be read by the initiated</note>, I must put forward the difficulties I once found in it. The first is that if it were true that this Writing made all great changes known, it would likewise announce the end of the world, as it is the greatest and most important of all changes; in this way, men could naturally know of it, which is against Holy Scripture. The second is that Astrologers have nonetheless predicted several of these changes with truth, without ever having understood this Writing; therefore, it would seem to be vain and imaginary. The third is that the arrangement of the Stars is not so essential to the shape of the letter assigned to it that the same star could not just as easily compose, for example, a ***Resh*** as a ***Daleth*** <note>These two Hebrew letters—ר and ד—are nearly identical, distinguished only by the sharpness of their corner</note>, and so on for all the others; and consequently, as each person forms different characters, one could derive a meaning entirely contrary to what another has found. 

But to all these difficulties, one can respond in this manner. To the first: it does not follow that this celestial Writing must show the end of the world, because God may have reserved this secret; or perhaps it truly will show it when the other signs recorded in the Gospels <note>literally "the Evangelists"</note> announce it, there being no more repugnance in saying that the Stars will show it through some writing than the Sun and Moon through some darkening. To the second: that the four causes which produce, according to the Astrologers, the greatest—

*Matthew 24:29*
*Mark 13:24*
*Luke 21:25*
*Cardan, Aphorism 1* <note>Referring to Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath and astrologer</note>
</margin>
